scenes.title: Foundation: limits and function behaviour
scenes.objective: Recall limits, continuity and derivatives before the theorems.

ask.q: What does lim x→a f(x)=L mean?
ask.nudge: Values of x close to a make f(x) close to L.

body: Continuity and differentiability are local properties. A limit describes the value approached by a function, not necessarily the value assigned at the point.
A function is continuous at a when the limit exists and equals f(a). Differentiability is stronger: it requires a finite limit of the difference quotient.

items.recall: f(a) is defined, lim x→a f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a).
refresh: Check the three parts separately: the function value exists, the two-sided limit exists, and both values agree. A removable hole violates the first or third part; a jump violates existence of the two-sided limit.
For a piecewise function, compute the left-hand limit, right-hand limit and the assigned value. Continuity requires all three to be equal.

items.ask: Write the derivative from first principles.
items.recall: f′(a)=lim h→0 [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h, when the finite limit exists.
refresh: The numerator is the change in the function and the denominator is the change in input. The quotient is an average rate of change; its limit is the instantaneous rate.
A finite derivative implies continuity, but continuity alone does not guarantee a derivative. The absolute-value function at zero is the standard counterexample.

items.ask: What does differentiability imply about continuity?
items.recall: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there; the converse is false.
refresh: If f′(a) exists, write f(a+h)−f(a)=h·[(f(a+h)−f(a))/h]. The bracket tends to a finite number and h tends to zero, so the difference tends to zero.
For f(x)=|x|, the function is continuous at zero, but the left derivative is −1 and the right derivative is +1. Hence it is not differentiable there.

scenes.title: Continuity is no break; differentiability is no corner
scenes.objective: Distinguish a connected graph from a smooth local slope.

ask.q: Is f(x)=|x| continuous and differentiable at zero?
ask.nudge: The graph has no jump, but what are the left and right slopes?

body: Continuity rules out a jump, a hole or an infinite break at the point. Differentiability additionally requires a unique finite tangent slope.
A sharp corner can be continuous but not differentiable. A vertical tangent may also prevent a finite derivative. A discontinuous function cannot be differentiable at that point.

scenes.title: Continuity: algebra and composition
scenes.objective: Use standard continuity rules and classify discontinuities.

ask.q: If f and g are continuous at a, when is f/g continuous at a?
ask.nudge: The denominator must not vanish at the point.

blocks.body: f is continuous at a iff lim(x→a)f(x)=f(a). Left and right limits must agree with the function value.
Sums, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous where defined. A quotient is continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero.
Removable: a finite limit exists but the value is missing or wrong. Jump: finite one-sided limits differ. Infinite: function grows without bound near the point.

steps.why: Use the branch valid to the left of 2.

steps.say: Compute the right-hand limit and point value.

steps.why: The common limit now equals f(2), so continuity holds.

scenario.teaser: A piecewise tariff must not jump at a threshold.
scenario.title: Choosing a threshold constant in a tariff function
body: A utility tariff may use one linear rate below a consumption threshold and a different formula above it. If the billing rule is intended to be continuous, the two formulas must agree at the threshold.
The algebra is exactly the one-sided-limit test: evaluate the left formula at the threshold, evaluate the right formula and the assigned value, then equate them.
A continuous tariff can still have a kink at the threshold. Continuity does not require equal left and right derivatives; that stronger condition would be needed for differentiability.

scenes.title: Differentiability and one-sided derivatives
scenes.objective: Test the derivative limit and identify corners.

ask.q: For f(x)=|x| at zero, what are the left and right derivatives?
ask.nudge: Evaluate the difference quotient on each side.

blocks.body: f′(a)=lim(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h. The two-sided limit must exist and be finite.
The left derivative is lim(h→0−) and the right derivative is lim(h→0+). Differentiability requires them to be equal and finite.
Differentiability ⇒ continuity. Continuity ⇏ differentiability. A corner, cusp, vertical tangent or discontinuity can prevent a finite derivative.

scenes.title: Guided: derivative from first principles
scenes.objective: Derive the derivative of a quadratic.
scenes.problem: Use first principles to differentiate f(x)=x² at x=a.
hints: Expand the square and cancel the common factor h.
Now let h tend to zero.

solution.say: The difference quotient is [(a+h)²−a²]/h=(2ah+h²)/h=2a+h. Its limit as h→0 is 2a.

scenes.title: Rolle's theorem
scenes.objective: Recognise and apply all three hypotheses.

ask.q: For f(x)=x²−1 on [−1,1], find a value c guaranteed by Rolle's theorem.
ask.nudge: The derivative is 2x and the endpoints have equal values.

blocks.body: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then there exists c∈(a,b) such that f′(c)=0.
Continuity is required on the CLOSED interval; differentiability is required only on the OPEN interval; endpoint values must be equal. If any condition fails, the theorem cannot be invoked.
A continuous curve that starts and ends at the same height and has no interior break must have at least one horizontal tangent.

scenes.title: Guided: apply the Mean Value Theorem
scenes.problem: Apply Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem to f(x)=x² on [1,3].

solution.say: The polynomial is continuous on [1,3] and differentiable on (1,3). The average slope is 4. Since f′(x)=2x, 2c=4 gives c=2, which lies in (1,3).

ask.q: Does MVT guarantee exactly one such c?
ask.nudge: The theorem guarantees at least one, not necessarily uniqueness.

scenes.title: Lagrange and Cauchy Mean Value Theorems
scenes.objective: State both theorems and distinguish their conclusions.

ask.q: What extra function appears in Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem?
ask.nudge: It compares the changes in two functions.

blocks.body: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then f′(c)=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a) for some c∈(a,b).
If f,g are continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then [f′(c)/g′(c)]=[f(b)−f(a)]/[g(b)−g(a)] for some c, under the usual non-zero denominator conditions.
Set g(x)=x in Cauchy's theorem to obtain Lagrange's MVT. Set f(a)=f(b) in Lagrange's theorem to obtain Rolle's theorem.

scenes.title: What the Mean Value Theorem really says
scenes.objective: Interpret the theorem as matching a tangent and a secant slope.

ask.q: If a journey's average speed is 60 km/h, what does the MVT say about instantaneous speed?
ask.nudge: At some time, the instantaneous speed equals the average, under the theorem's smoothness conditions.

body: The secant line joins the two endpoint values. The MVT guarantees at least one interior tangent parallel to that secant, so the instantaneous derivative equals the average rate of change.
It does not say the point is unique, nor does it identify its location without solving an equation. It is an existence theorem, not a numerical approximation rule.

scenario.teaser: Average speed and instantaneous speed meet somewhere.
scenario.title: The average-speed interpretation
body: A vehicle travels a smooth position function s(t) over a time interval. Its average velocity is [s(b)−s(a)]/(b−a).
If s is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable inside it, the Mean Value Theorem guarantees some intermediate time c where the instantaneous velocity s′(c) equals that average velocity.
This is a mathematical existence statement. It does not mean the speed is constant, and it does not identify the time c without further information about s(t).

scenes.objective: Reject an invalid MVT application correctly.

ask.q: Can MVT be applied to f(x)=1/x on [−1,1]?
ask.nudge: Check continuity on the whole closed interval.

scenes.problem: Decide whether Rolle's theorem applies to f(x)=1/x on [−1,1].

steps.why: They are not equal, so the endpoint condition fails.

steps.say: Check continuity on the closed interval.
steps.why: The function is not continuous on [−1,1].
Two hypotheses fail. Do not claim a theorem conclusion merely because the endpoint values are available.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there.
items.why: The difference quotient proof establishes this implication.
|x| is continuous but not differentiable at zero.

items.claim: Rolle requires differentiability at both endpoints.
items.why: Differentiability is required only on the open interval.

items.claim: The MVT guarantees at least one interior point.
items.why: It is an existence theorem; uniqueness is not guaranteed.

items.claim: If a hypothesis fails, the theorem's conclusion must be false.
items.why: The theorem is simply unavailable; the conclusion may still happen for another reason.

scenes.title: Final theorem checklist
scenes.objective: Select and apply the right theorem.
body: 1. Continuity at a: limit exists and equals f(a).
2. Differentiability: the finite two-sided difference-quotient limit exists.
3. Differentiability implies continuity; continuity does not imply differentiability.
4. Rolle: continuous [a,b], differentiable (a,b), equal endpoint values; conclude f′(c)=0.
5. Lagrange MVT: same continuity and differentiability; conclude f′(c) equals the secant slope.
6. Cauchy MVT compares the derivative ratio of two functions with their endpoint-change ratio.
7. Verify every hypothesis before invoking any theorem.
